weakness: The only grasp was a tilted pinch around the cup's upper body, sized for a 5 cm cup. On a cup 7-8 cm wide the 9 cm gripper had almost no clearance: the approach knocked the cup over, or the angled pads wedged it out of the hand on the lift. The fallback (the cup's annotated rim points) only had near-vertical approaches, which were unreachable for cups far from the robot.
how_found: Questioned A5 (the cup is small and cup-shaped), because real cups and mugs vary in size; screening showed that a mug-sized cup (1.5x) drops the pipeline from 1.0 to 0.0, while clutter around the coaster, a moving coaster and a heavy cup did not break it.
why_missed: Phase 1 only saw the task's own cup models, all 4.9-5.5 cm wide, so the grasp was tuned to them and the object's size was never compared with the gripper's opening.
fix: Measure the cup's width and choose the grasp from it: a body grasp only if width + 2.5 cm fits the 9 cm opening, otherwise a rim pinch. The rim pinch tries the annotated rim points, then a tilted pinch of the wall facing the hand (55-85 deg, several azimuths, opening 0.5 so the inner finger clears the far wall). The back-out direction after release is read from the hand pose, so it works for either grasp.
general_rule: Choose the grasp from the object's measured size relative to the gripper opening (with clearance for perception noise), and keep a second grasp family that stays reachable when the first one is not.

weakness: When light objects stood 1.5 cm from the cup on every side, every approach was refused, and the pipeline kept searching more approach angles, arms and grasp types until the 120 s budget ran out. It never moved anything out of the way. Each grasp candidate also re-opened an already open gripper (~1 s), so the search alone used most of the time.
how_found: Questioned A2 (some approach to the cup is always free), because real tables are cluttered around cups. Screening: four movable boxes packed around the cup gave 0.0; fixed walls around the cup also gave 0.0, but probably leave no room for the gripper at all, so they were not gated.
why_missed: In Phase 1 the cup always stood on open table, and a refused motion was only ever answered with a different approach angle, never with a change to the scene.
fix: Find small movable objects within 7 cm of the cup (from get_obstacles, size-filtered so furniture is never moved). Clear the ones on the hand's side first, up to 3: a top-down grasp closing across the axis perpendicular to the cup, then set it down at a free reachable spot away from the cup, the coaster and the path between them. If one cannot be grasped, try the next. On the short final approaches, brushing the remaining light neighbours is allowed (their gaps are inside the planner's margin). Gripper motions that would change nothing are skipped.
general_rule: If the target is boxed in by small movable objects, move them to a free spot before grasping instead of searching more and more approach angles until the time runs out.

weakness: Each grasp was planned from one estimate of the cup taken before the arm moved, and every fallback candidate reused that estimate. A cup that slid 9 cm while the arm approached made every attempt close on empty space or knock the cup, until the time ran out. Nothing checked that the cup was still where the grasp had been planned.
how_found: Questioned A4 (the cup stays where it was estimated during the approach), because people and other actions move objects. Screening needed care: a plain push tipped the cup in this simulator (high default friction), so the push was combined with a slick cup and table, which let the cup slide 9 cm upright. A no-push control on the same slick surfaces scored 0.8, so the motion, not the slickness, broke the pipeline (0.0).
why_missed: In Phase 1 and the earlier rounds the cup never moved by itself, so one estimate per grasp sequence was always valid.
fix: Before clearing or grasping, wait until two averaged estimates 0.5 s apart agree within 1.5 cm (the cup is still). Right after reaching each pre-grasp pose, estimate again; if the cup moved more than 1.5 cm, abort, wait until it is still and replan from its new position. To keep the earlier crowded-cup variation within the time budget with these extra checks, objects are cleared with whichever arm reaches them, one at a time between grasp attempts, and set down with a quick lift-shift-lower instead of a full placement search.
general_rule: Re-measure the target right before the irreversible part of an approach and replan if it has moved; never reuse one estimate for a whole sequence of attempts.

weakness: The pipeline assumed the cup stands upright. A cup lying on its side was carried to the coaster and set down lying, so its base centre (what the check measures) ended 3-4 cm off; nothing noticed that the object first had to be turned upright.
how_found: Questioned A5 again from the orientation side, because cups get knocked over; screening gave 0.0 for a cup lying on its side, while an object lying on the coaster, a coaster at the back of the table and a divider between cup and coaster did not break the pipeline.
why_missed: Every earlier scene had the cup standing, so 'grasp' and 'place' were written for one orientation, with no step that checks or changes the object's orientation.
fix: Not recovered within 6 repairs (best 0.7; the round-3 pipeline is kept). Tried: (1) plan the final upright tilted grasp and map it back through the stand-up rotation -- no reachable candidate, because with the rim pointing away from the robot every downward final approach maps to an approach from the far side; (2) flip: top-down grasp across the lying cup, lift, quarter turn about the closing axis in whichever direction keeps the hand reachable (the cup may end on its base or rim), set down, regrasp -- worked in isolation, 0.5 in the full run; (3-5) tilted and shifted flip grasps, a cap on refused approaches, flipping only clearly lying cups, a higher grasp -- 0.3, 0.4, 0.7; (6) carry the stood-up cup straight to the coaster -- 0.4. The remaining failures were cups at the back or edge of the table where no flip grasp is reachable, episodes that ran out of the 120 s budget (stand-up plus pick-and-place is roughly twice the motion), and occasional cups flung by the physics during the turn. A flip test also showed that box extents cannot tell a squat cup's axis from a diameter; the axis has to come from the detected frame.
general_rule: Check an object's orientation before manipulating it, and if it must be turned, choose the turn direction and the grasp from reachability and budget the extra motions (re-orienting costs about as much as the whole pick-and-place) before committing.

weakness: Clutter was only cleared around the object to pick, never around the place to put it down. With light objects packed around the coaster, the cup could not be lowered between them, or tipped against them, and the pipeline ran out of time. Two more weaknesses showed while repairing: a fully opened gripper swung its fingers into neighbours at release and knocked the cup; and a 'not quite centred' check on noisy estimates restarted a pick-and-place that could not finish in the remaining time, so placements already inside the success tolerance ended with the cup in a closed hand.
how_found: Questioned A1 (nothing next to the coaster) after round 2 had covered the pick side; screening gave 0.2. The first design (v5) was rejected by the validity gate: on one seed of ten, a box started inside the furniture.
why_missed: The clearing added in round 2 was written for the pick only; the placement path and the end-of-task correction were never tested with neighbours close by or with little time left.
fix: Before picking (both hands free), clear up to 2 light objects crowding the coaster, with the round-2 routine generalised to any target; brush the rest on the final descent. Grasp boxes 4.5 cm below their top and check they are still held after the lift (a 2.5 cm pinch slipped and the same box was 'cleared' twice). Release with the gripper opened only to the cup's width + 1.5 cm. Re-place only if a 16-sample estimate is off by more than 1.2 cm AND at least 45 s of the 120 s remain. Grasp the cup body lower (0.15 of its height above centre) so a slick cup swings less. Six repairs were needed; each full check varied by about 0.2 per scene between runs.
general_rule: Clear the spot where an object will be put down as well as where it is picked up, before picking it up while the hands are free; and never start a corrective retry that cannot finish in the remaining time, because a near miss with an open hand beats a timed-out retry holding the object.

weakness: Each grasp and lift assumed free space above the cup: lifting was always straight up, and refused approaches were retried without limit. With the cup at the back of the table next to a low bookcase, the straight lift was refused, the 'held' cup was lost, and eight near-identical refused re-approaches (~6 s each) used up the time.
how_found: Questioned A10 (one arm comfortably reaches both objects) with the cup at the back on one side and the coaster at the front edge on the other; screening gave 0.4 and the gate 0.5.
why_missed: Earlier scenes never put the cup next to furniture, so lifting straight up and retrying approaches were always cheap.
fix: Not recovered (one repair, 0.3); the round-5 pipeline is kept. The repair backed away along the approach when the straight lift was refused, and gave up an arm after 4 refused final approaches. It stopped there because the variation is flawed: the furniture layout changes with the seed, and in 5 of 10 seeds the fixed cup position (0.10, 0.12) lies inside the low bookcase's footprint (4-5 cm overlap in x and y), i.e. in its lower compartment under a fixed overhang. The validity check did not catch this, since nothing interpenetrates. Those 5 seeds are a different task that the padded planner cannot approach, so 0.8 was unreachable whatever the pipeline did; the other failures were cups tipping at a coaster very close to the robot.
general_rule: When placing objects at fixed coordinates in scenes whose furniture moves between instances, check every instance for containment under furniture, not just collisions; and retry a refused approach only a few times, then change strategy instead of repeating it until the time runs out.

weakness: The cup's width was taken from the world-axis extent of its detected box. For a cup turned about 45 deg this overestimates the diameter by up to 41% (0.12 m for a 7.3-8.3 cm mug). So the grasp choice and the clutter gaps were computed from a cup that seemed much wider than it was. Mild in open scenes (some normal cups were sent rim-first), but with a mug-size cup boxed in by light objects, nothing fitted and the time ran out.
how_found: After nine single-axis screenings in this round failed to break the pipeline, combined two axes that had each broken and recovered (a mug-size cup and packed clutter); screening gave 0.3. A profile of one failure printed the cup width the pipeline used, which was far larger than the cup.
why_missed: The width helper was written in round 1 and only ever checked on cups that happened to be nearly axis-aligned; its result was never compared with the object's known size.
fix: Measure the width in the object's own frame: the larger of the two box extents that are not the vertical axis. One repair: base 0.9, v1 0.9, v2 0.8, v3 0.8, v6 0.9, v8 0.8.
general_rule: Measure an object's size in its own frame, not from its world-axis bounding box, before using it to choose a grasp or a clearance, and sanity-check derived sizes against what the object can plausibly be.
